title: Iran War Drains US Munitions to 'Beyond Critical' as Russia Tests Mobile ICBM and India Opens Missile Production to Private Industry
subhead: A Wall Street Journal report says the six-month Iran war has depleted US Patriot and ATACMS stocks in Europe to 'beyond critical' levels, forcing European Command to adjust plans and raising doubts about Taiwan contingency readiness — while Russia test-launched a mobile ICBM and India moved to break state monopoly on missile production.

sections.heading: US Munitions Drain From Iran War Strains Global Deterrence
sections.body: The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that the six-month Iran war has severely depleted US military stockpiles, limiting Washington's ability to deter China and Russia. According to the report, inventories in Europe of PAC-3 Patriot interceptors and Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) are considered at 'beyond critical' levels, with THAAD anti-missile interceptors and counter-drone systems also redirected to the Middle East. US officials assessed Washington could not fully execute contingency plans to defend Taiwan in the short term, and moving air-defense units from Japan, South Korea and Germany to the Middle East has created 'soft spots' in the global posture that could take years to refill. The White House and Pentagon denied a munitions shortage, saying the military maintains enough resources for all of President Trump's goals.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the clearest signal yet that the Iran war is consuming the US arsenal faster than industry can replace it — a constraint that directly shapes deterrence credibility in the Pacific and Europe, not just the Middle East.

sections.heading: NATO Disputes Severity as Patriot Stocks Fall
sections.body: Two US and NATO officials told the Associated Press that Patriot interceptor stocks in Europe had fallen sharply, with one US defense official describing the situation as 'beyond critical.' NATO military spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell disputed that assessment, saying it was 'simply not the case' that Patriot stocks in Europe were beyond critical. The disagreement matters because NATO itself says it needs 'many more' interceptors, sensors and command-and-control capabilities, per Deputy Secretary General Radmila Šekerinska, who stressed the urgency of expanding production and procurement. The Iran war has added further pressure to air and missile-defense resources already stretched by Ukraine demand.
sections.whyItMatters: The public split between US and NATO officials over the severity of the shortfall reflects a deeper tension: allies are being asked to trust a defense posture whose stockpiles are visibly thinning, and the interceptor production base cannot keep pace with two simultaneous high-intensity demands.

sections.heading: Russia Test-Launches Mobile ICBM Days After CIA Chief's Moscow Visit
sections.body: Russia's Strategic Missile Forces conducted a successful combat training launch of a mobile, solid-fuel intercontinental ballistic missile from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in the Arkhangelsk region, with the missile traveling more than 6,700 kilometers to the Kura test site on the Kamchatka Peninsula, the Defence Ministry announced Friday. The launch deployed a mobile transporter-erector-launcher battery into a remote forested area before firing — a demonstration of the survivability of Russia's land-based nuclear triad, which relies on systems such as the mobile RS-24 Yars, silo-based RS-28 Sarmat and legacy Topol-M. The test came days after CIA Director John Ratcliffe's reported Moscow visit, per the Kyiv Post.
sections.whyItMatters: The timing and mobile-launch format are a deliberate strategic signal: Moscow is underscoring the survivability of its nuclear deterrent at a moment of high tension, and doing so immediately after a rare US intelligence chief visit frames the test as a warning rather than routine maintenance.

sections.heading: India Opens Conventional Missile Production to Private Industry
sections.body: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh cleared the transfer of technologies (ToT) developed by the DRDO for all conventional missile systems to Indian defense companies for domestic production, the New Indian Express reports. The order terminates Bharat Dynamics Limited's (BDL) de facto monopoly as prime integrator of tactical missiles and lifts production out of the nomination system, allowing bidding among private firms to be designated development-cum-production partners (DcPP). India's strategic inventory — the Agni series and sea-based deterrent — stays outside the dispensation, as do systems held in joint ventures like BrahMos and the Indo-Israeli MRSAM. BDL remains the most experienced manufacturer but no longer has an automatic mandate.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a structural shift in India's defense industrial base: by injecting competition into missile production, New Delhi aims to scale output and draw MSMEs into the supply chain — a move that matters for both domestic readiness and India's growing arms-export ambitions.

sections.heading: India Simplifies Defense Export Rules, Expands OGEL Access
sections.body: The Department of Defence Production introduced reforms to simplify India's Defence Export SOP and Open General Export Licence (OGEL) framework, per Business World. Stakeholder consultation is no longer required for exports of non-lethal items to most destinations, and consultation is removed for all eligible items in international tenders and exhibitions. Three existing OGEL SOPs were consolidated into one, validity extended from two to three years, and coverage expanded from 41 countries to all countries except negative or sensitive destinations and those under UNSC sanctions or arms embargoes. The reforms come as India's defense production hit an all-time high of Rs 1.78 lakh crore, with exports at a record Rs 38,424 crore in FY 2025-26.
sections.whyItMatters: India is deliberately removing friction from its export regime to convert a record production base into a global arms-export business — a direct challenge to established suppliers and a sign New Delhi sees defense exports as a strategic and economic priority.

sections.heading: TKMS Nears $9B Indian Submarine Deal as Berlin Halts F126 Frigate
sections.body: German shipbuilder thyssenkrupp Marine Systems (TKMS) is closing in on a roughly $9 billion deal with India under Project 75(I) for six conventional submarines, built in partnership with Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, per Ad-hoc-news. The company's total order backlog has swelled to more than €25 billion, with nine-month revenue up 19 percent to €1.89 billion and EBIT margin guidance raised to as much as 6.5 percent. The momentum is clouded by Berlin's halt of the F126 frigate program over significant cost overruns, and TKMS has challenged reported €40 billion F127 cost estimates. In Canada, TKMS is the preferred bidder for a submarine program centered on the Class 212CD design, with first delivery possible by 2033.
sections.whyItMatters: TKMS embodies the two-sided reality of the European naval boom: record export demand and order books are colliding with domestic cost overruns and procurement friction, testing whether European shipbuilders can convert demand into sustainable production.

sections.heading: North Korea Reshuffles Defense Leadership; UK Shelves 3% Spending Target
sections.body: North Korea replaced its defense minister in a reshuffle of senior military leadership, state media reported Sunday. Kim Song-gi, director of the General Political Bureau of the Korean People's Army, was appointed defense minister, replacing No Kwang-chol, who was moved to first vice-director of the Munitions Industry Department, per Yonhap and KCNA. Separately, the FT Weekend reported Chancellor John Healey will 'shelve' his target of spending 3 percent of GDP on defense by 2030 when he sets out his first Budget in October, delaying bigger decisions until a Treasury review next year — drawing accusations of hypocrisy from ex-defense ministers and prompting the Daily Telegraph to report Washington is considering using the Falkland Islands as leverage to pressure the UK on defense spending.
sections.whyItMatters: North Korea's move of its former defense minister into the munitions industry role signals a continued focus on weapons production capacity, while the UK's shelved spending target — and the US response — shows the burden-sharing debate is now being enforced with direct pressure rather than persuasion.

bottomLine: The dominant story today is the cost of the Iran war: a Wall Street Journal report that US Patriot and ATACMS stocks in Europe are 'beyond critical' and that Taiwan contingency plans cannot be fully executed in the short term — a claim the Pentagon denies but NATO itself does not fully rebut. Russia's mobile ICBM test, timed days after the CIA chief's Moscow visit, reinforces the deterrence backdrop. Meanwhile, India moved decisively to open conventional missile production to private industry and simplify its export regime, and TKMS neared a $9 billion Indian submarine deal even as Berlin halted a frigate program. The through-line: high-intensity conflict is consuming stockpiles faster than industry can rebuild them, and the states best positioned to scale production — India, and increasingly Turkey — are the ones converting that pressure into industrial advantage.
sources: Wall Street Journal (via Turkiye Today), Outlook India, Associated Press, WION, Kyiv Post, New Indian Express, Business World, Ad-hoc-news, Yonhap, KCNA, BBC, Financial Times, Daily Telegraph, Daily Mail, Airdata News
